claim: We must support the Scottish Independence

roles.A: You are a neutral evidence analyst. Seek the strongest relevant facts on both sides.
roles.B: You are a neutral evidence analyst. Seek the strongest relevant facts on both sides.
roles.C: You are a neutral evidence analyst. Seek the strongest relevant facts on both sides.

evidence.text: States are often seen as having one single unitary interest, however this is not the case the interests of different regions can be very different. It should therefore not be surprising that Scotland and rUK have different interests with relation to the EU. For example on climate change Scotland has the greatest potential for the generation of renewable energy in Europe with 25% of Europe’s tidal potential and 10% of wave potential yet the UK is in favour of scrapping European targets for the generation of renewable energy.

Many of Scotland’s problems are grounded in the fact that its potential has consistently been held back. Because the focus for economic development from a Westminster perspective has focused for generations on North Sea oil and the coal fields of Lanarkshire, huge opportunities were missed and the best and the brightest tended be dragged down south for jobs worthy of their skills. Even with the limited powers allowed by devolution a burgeoning life-sciences sector, a growing IT sector in silicon glen are adding to the traditional industries. Since 2003 Scotland has generally had faster economic growth than the UK with 13% during the period from 2003-2007 compared to the UK’s 11.4%.

The Barnett established the model by which money is divided up within the regions and nations of the UK. The formula works greatly to Scotland’s advantage with a net flow of funding heading north. The English taxpayer subsidizes Scots to the tune of £19bn a year (2009-10). Scotland needs English support financially just as she does in terms of diplomatic representation or political muscle.

For over three centuries the two nations have cooperated much to their mutual advantage. The majority of Scots are happy with their British-ness. In terms of culture and art the two nations have maintained distinctive traditions but ones which have been enhanced by their interaction. There are many people who have relatives from Scotland and another of the Home Nations for whom British is the more obvious identity.

gold_perspectives.text: An independent Scotland has enormous economic potential to join other small European nations, especially as a leader in technology and renewable energy
Scotland has a proud history and has demonstrated since devolution different political interests
Scotland needs English economic muscle as through the Barnett formula England, especially the Southeast effectively subsidizes the rest of the UK in general and Scotland in particular
The union has worked for over three hundred years and most people feel comfortable with the joint Scots/British identity

transcript.A|1:
E1 and E2 offer empirical grounds for independence: Scotland has distinct EU interests, major renewable potential, and faster growth than the UK in 2003–2007. E3 undermines the claim: Scotland receives a net financial subsidy from England, about £19bn in 2009–10, plus diplomatic and political support. E4 also undermines it: three centuries of mutual cooperation, majority Scottish satisfaction with British identity, and mixed family ties make independence less clearly necessary.

The claim is normative (“must”), while the dossier supplies both supporting and opposing empirical facts. No evidence establishes that independence is required, only that there are trade-offs.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
transcript.B|1:
E1 shows divergent EU interests and Scottish renewable potential, but this is a sectoral argument, not proof independence is necessary. E2 cites faster Scottish growth 2003–2007 and missed opportunities, supporting capacity for self-government, yet this is partial and dated. E3 directly undermines the claim: Scotland receives an estimated £19bn net subsidy from English taxpayers, implying fiscal vulnerability. E4 notes three centuries of mutual benefit and widespread British identity, challenging the “must” imperative. The dossier contains no evidence on currency, defence, EU membership terms, or post-independence fiscal sustainability. The claim is a value judgment; the evidence is mixed and insufficient to establish that independence is compelled.

VERDICT: UNCERTAIN
transcript.C|1:

The evidence suggests a trade-off, not a necessity.

Because the focus for economic development from a Westminster perspective has focused for generations on North Sea oil and the coal fields of Lanarkshire, huge opportunities were missed and the best and the brightest tended be dragged down south for jobs worthy of their skills. Even with the limited powers allowed by devolution a burgeoning life-sciences sector, a growing IT sector in silicon glen are adding to the traditional industries. Since 2003 Scotland has generally had faster economic growth than the UK with 13% during the period from 2003-2007 compared to the UK’s 11.4%.

[E3] The Barnett established the model by which money is divided up within the regions and nations of the UK. The formula works greatly to Scotland’s advantage with a net flow of funding heading north. The English taxpayer subsidizes Scots to the tune of £19bn a year (2009-10). Scotland needs English support financially just as she does in terms of diplomatic representation or political muscle.

[E4] For over three centuries the two nations have cooperated much to their mutual advantage. The majority of Scots are happy with their British-ness. In terms of culture and art the two nations have maintained distinctive traditions but ones which have been enhanced by their interaction. There are many people who have relatives from Scotland and another of the Home Nations for whom British is the more obvious identity.
